newsitem.title: USA: Clinton resists pressure to stop UPS strike.
newsitem.headline: Clinton resists pressure to stop UPS strike.

text.p: President Bill Clinton resisted pressure from U.S. companies to intervene in the United Parcel Service strike Wednesday, saying the impact of the walkout was not severe enough to warrant his direct involvement.

A group including chief executives from Sears, Kmart and other big retailers called on the president to intervene in the walkout, now in its third day, warning that a prolonged strike could hurt economic growth.
The U.S. Chamber of Commerce warned of "irreparable harm and massive layoffs" for small- and mid-size firms if 185,000 striking Teamsters were not ordered back to work at UPS.

"The economy, which is enjoying unprecedented sustained growth, could experience a sudden downward spiral if this strike continues for an extended period," the National Retail Federation said in a letter to Clinton signed by 36 industry executives.
UPS said at least 50,000 letters seeking Clinton's assistance in the strike had been mailed to the White House by customers, members of Congress and state governors.

But the president told a White House news conference he could only halt the strike by invoking the Taft-Hartley Law on industrial relations, which authorises the nation's chief executive to halt strikes that threaten health and safety.
"There has to be a severe damage to the country. The test is ... very high before the president can intervene," he said.

With UPS handling less than 10 percent of its normal shipments and no new talks scheduled, the strike has meant rising shipping costs and logistical nightmares for businesses, manufacturers and consumers who rely on UPS.

Sport-Haley Inc., for example, a Denver-based sportswear maker, told investors that a prolonged work stoppage could hurt its earnings by driving up shipping costs. Its stock tumbled $2.50 to $13.75 on Nasdaq, a drop of 15 percent.

The National Retail Federation sought to illustrate the strike's potential economic impact by noting that U.S. retails sales amount to $2.5 trillion and account for about one-third of the economy. About $50 billion of that is from catalogue and mail order retailers that rely heavily on UPS.

As the world's largest parcel delivery company, UPS controls 80 percent of the U.S. parcel delivery business, normally handling 12 million packages a day. Its daily volume equals 6 percent of gross domestic product.

Thousands of Teamsters, including drivers, package sorters and loaders, spent a third day on picket lines from Maine to California. They had backing from 2,000 unionized UPS pilots who have refused to cross Teamster picket lines.
Meanwhile, 50,000 non-union workers scrambled to keep parts of the huge UPS network running.
UPS, with annual sales of $22.4 billion, also said in a filing with securities regulators that the first national strike in its 90-year history would hurt earnings and probably cost it customers.
On Tuesday, Labour Secretary Alexis Herman urged UPS Chief Executive James Kelly and Teamster President Ron Carey to go back to the bargaining table.
Carey said he was ready to meet UPS management "anywhere, anytime." But the company refused to budge from what it called its last, best offer that the union rejected last week.
"We are ready to go back to the table. But our position hasn't changed about our offer. We've made our last, best and final offer," UPS spokesman Norman Black said.

The Teamsters said they struck early on Monday after the company refused to to create thousands of new full-time jobs each year from part-time jobs, which account for 60 percent of the Atlanta-based company's 301,000 domestic workers.

UPS called those issues "a smoke screen," saying the real issue was the Teamsters' refusal to consider a company request to withdraw from a multi-employer pension plan that includes 30 other companies, mostly trucking firms. UPS says the plan would boost pension benefits to its Teamster employees.
The union says the multi-employer plan shields its members from any one company's financial problems.

"This is a fight that's been existing for many years about good decent jobs, about being treated fairly, about protections from pensions, about building an America that works for everyone," Carey said on Cable News Network.
